#Text=Carrots, Parsnips, and Beetroot are distinguished among
#Text= vegetables for their richness in sugar.
#Text=Bread has heen made
#Text= from all of them.
#Text=When in great abundance they are
#Text= sometimes used in distilleries for making spirits.
#Text=Carrots should be light red or yellow, of a regular conical
#Text= shape, sweet and crisp.
#Text=Young carrots are more tender and
#Text= are preferred for the table.
#Text=They are in season from April
#Text= till June.
#Text=Parsnips should be buff in colour, unforked in the roots,
#Text= sweet and crisp.
#Text=They are in season winter and spring.
#Text=They should be stored in dry sand.
#Text=Beetroot should be deep red, or purple, of a long oval or
#Text= globular shape, fine-grained, sweet and delicate in flavour.
#Text=It keeps well in dry sand, and is always seasonable.
#Text=The larvce of the carrot-fly burrow into and spoil carrots
#Text= and parsnips, often causing them to shrivel.
#Text=A mildew also
#Text= attacks parsnip roots.
#Text=Beetroot is liable to be damaged by
#Text= a nematode — the male of which is like a worm, the female
#Text= lemon-shaped.
#Text=Celery should be nearly white in colour, large, crisp,
#Text= solid, and nutty in flavour.
#Text=It is in season in winter and
#Text= spring.
#Text=It is fit for use for some time after being gathered.
#Text=There is a variety of celery in which the root is large and
#Text= turnip-shaped.

#Text=Much damage is done to the plant by the larva of the

#Text=Mushrooms may be gathered in the fields in September
#Text= and October, and forced mushrooms can be obtained all the
#Text= year round.
#Text=There are many edible British species.

#Text=The bread may be unleavened or it may be
#Text= aerated with leaven or yeast, by kneading the flour with
#Text= water charged with carbonic acid, or by means of a baking
#Text= powder or a chemical compound.
#Text=Thus, bread includes
#Text= oat cakes, passover cakes, water biscuits, black or rye bread,
#Text= &c.
#Text=The word is, however, in this country usually restricted
#Text= to wheaten bread leavened, fermented, or aerated.
#Text=Good wheaten bread should be well baked (not burnt),
#Text= light and spongy, the crumb being well permeated with little
#Text= cavities.
#Text=It should be thoroughly kneaded, of good colour
#Text= (white or brown), not acid to the taste, not bitter, not too
#Text= moist.
#Text=When set aside, the lower part should not become
#Text= sodden.
#Text=A 4-lb. loaf loses about ij oz. in twenty-four
#Text= hours, about 5 oz. in forty-eight hours, and about 7 oz. in
#Text= sixty hours.
#Text=This loss will vary with the temperature,
#Text= draughts of air, &c.

#Text= Bread may have many defects.
#Text=It may be sodden and
#Text= heavy owing to bad flour or yeast, the sponge never having
#Text= risen properly, or owing to imperfect baking.
#Text=It may be
#Text= sour owing to bad flour, or to fermentation having been
#Text= allowed to proceed too far.
#Text=A slight degree of sourness in
#Text= leavened bread is not objected to.
#Text=It may be bitter owing
#Text= to bitter yeast.
#Text=Finally, it may be mouldy, which is due
#Text= to the bread having been too moist originally, having been
#Text= kept in a damp place, or kept too long, or to bad flour
#Text= having been used.
#Text=Wheaten bread may be adulterated with barley, maize,
#Text= pea or bean flour, and with boiled rice or potatoes.

#Text=After the milk is

#Text= and the remainder of the milk is less opaque, and nearly or
#Text= quite white.

#Text=Sour Milk. — Under the influence of an organism  ' called
#Text= the bacillus of lactic acid) introduced from without, the
#Text= sugar of milk is converted into lactic acid, and it is this
#Text= which causes milk to turn sour.
#Text=Milk only slightly soured,
#Text= exposed or offered for sale as "milk," may be seized as
#Text= unsound, and an application for an order to destroy it
#Text= applied for.
#Text=However, butter-milk is ordinarily sold some-
#Text= what "turned;" sour butter-milk may therefore be held to
#Text= be the normal condition of butter-milk.
#Text=When milk sours,
#Text= the part that forms the cheese, the casein, coagulates.
#Text=In
#Text= fresh milk the casein is combined with phosphate of lime,
#Text= which keeps it fluid.
#Text=The acid converts the neutral alkaline
#Text= phosphate into an acid phosphate, and the casein coagulates.
#Text=Warmth, as is well known, assists the change — thus milk in
#Text= which only a very little lactic acid has been formed may
#Text= appear perfectly fresh when cool and yet curdle on boiling

#Text=The cream,
#Text= which contains casein and milk-liquid as well as fat, is
#Text= ordinarily removed by skimming, and violently shaken or
#Text= beaten up in a churn or other suitable vessel, till the fat
#Text= globules unite and form a mass.
#Text=This mass, carefully

#Text= is the butter of commerce.
#Text=Butter varies much in colour, flavour, and quality.
#Text=The
#Text= colour ranges, according to the season and the food and
#Text= breed of the cow, from deep yellow to almost white.
#Text=The
#Text= flavour is influenced by the food of the cow and the quality
#Text= by the state of the cream, the method of churning and
#Text= making up the butter, &c.
#Text=Carefully prepared butter has a pleasant odour and
#Text= agreeable taste, and is of the same consistency and colour
#Text= throughout.
#Text=It is easily cut and moulded into shapes, and
#Text= melts to a light coloured oil.
#Text=It always contains water and

#Text=The curd is especially

#Text=Butter fat, freed from curd and

#Text=It seems superfluous to say that butter of fine flavour

#Text=Cinnamon has a sweet taste and
#Text= an aromatic flavour.
#Text=It is light brown in colour, well
#Text= curled, and scarcely thicker than drawing paper.
#Text=It
#Text= breaks with an uneven fibrous margin.
#Text=It contains a
#Text= volatile oil, tannin, mucilage, colouring matter, resin, an
#Text= acrid principle, woody fibre, starch, and a little moisture.
#Text=Cassia, the bark of another tree belonging to the laurel
#Text= family, is sometimes substituted for cinnamon.
#Text=Cassia bark

#Text= is brown, much stouter than cinnamon, and breaks short off,
#Text= without splintering.
#Text=Cassia is also redder in colour and
#Text= stronger in taste, but less sweet.
#Text=It contains two brown-coloured hemispherical seeds, having
#Text= an aromatic taste and odour.
#Text=The seed-vessels, or pods, of
#Text= cardamom are of triangular form, each containing several
#Text= hard, reddish-brown seeds, having a pungent taste, and
#Text= popularly known as "grains of paradise."
#Text=Cumin and fenu-
#Text= greek seeds are aromatic seeds having a peculiar medicinal
#Text= taste and odour.
#Text=The characteristic flavour of curry is due
#Text= largely to the cumin it contains.
#Text=Curry has been found to
#Text= be adulterated with ground rice, potato starch, common salt,
#Text= red lead, and ferruginous earths.

#Text= bland taste.

#Text=Good lime juice or
